JSON: Name: gtpbp1_decoding_pipeline Title: Time-resolved cryo-electron microscopy and complementary biochemical assays to determine how GTPBP1 structural elements control decoding kinetics and fidelity on mammalian 80S ribosomes Short Hypothesis: The N-terminal domain and shoulder-interacting H-loop of GTPBP1 sterically restrict post-GTP-hydrolysis interdomain rearrangements, causing prolonged GTPBP1 residence on the ribosome that increases proofreading time and thereby reduces near-cognate tRNA accommodation and misincorporation relative to eEF1A. Related Work: Structural and kinetic studies of translational GTPases (EF-Tu, eEF1A) have shown that small-subunit conformational changes and G-domain repositioning toward the SRL couple codon recognition to rapid GTP hydrolysis and factor dissociation. Time-resolved and ensemble cryo-EM, single-molecule, and biochemical assays established kinetic proofreading models in which rapid post-hydrolysis EF dissociation enables tRNA accommodation, while slowed dissociation increases fidelity. Prior biochemical work reported that GTPBP1 binds aa-tRNA and catalyzes elongation with slower peptide-bond formation and can deliver deacylated tRNA; however, the molecular features that produce slow dissociation and their causal effect on accuracy were unresolved. Predictions and limited structural models indicated unique GTPBP1 elements (extended N-domain, H-loop replacing α2 helix, K+-binding pocket) and suggested divergence from GTPBP2, but the functional consequences of these differences, and whether they directly modulate kinetic proofreading and decoding fidelity, remain untested. Abstract: GTP-binding protein 1 (GTPBP1) is a mammalian translational GTPase reported to deliver aminoacyl-tRNA to ribosomes while exhibiting unusually slow post-GTP-hydrolysis dissociation and elevated decoding accuracy. The molecular basis linking GTPBP1 architecture to slowed dissociation and increased fidelity is unresolved. We propose an integrated experimental pipeline combining time-resolved cryo-electron microscopy, quantitative biochemical kinetics, single-molecule assays, and targeted mutagenesis to test whether specific GTPBP1 elements (N-terminal domain, H-loop, and a K+-binding pocket) sterically or electrostatically inhibit post-hydrolysis interdomain rearrangements and thereby extend proofreading windows. The main contribution will be a causal, residue-level mapping between structural features and decoding kinetics, producing mechanistic metrics (GTP hydrolysis, dissociation, accommodation, misincorporation rates) and structural state occupancies. Expected outcomes include identification of GTPBP1 determinants that increase decoding fidelity, experimental validation of predicted functional differences from eEF1A/GTPBP2, and a framework for interpreting disease-associated GTPBP1 variants. These results will clarify how a specialized GTPase modulates translational accuracy and quality-control pathways. Experiments: Overview: parallel structural and functional assays testing wild-type human GTPBP1, targeted mutants, eEF1A (reference), and GTPBP2 (comparison) on mammalian 80S ribosomes. Samples/datasets: (1) Cryo-EM: time-resolved datasets at GDPCP and at GTP 0s, 30s, 1min, 5min with purified rabbit reticulocyte 80S programmed with reporter mRNAs containing cognate and near-cognate codons (e.g., UCU vs UCC Ser codons) and P-site Met-tRNA; target particle counts ≥200k per condition. (2) Biochemical kinetics: single-turnover GTP hydrolysis (radiometric or Pi release), stopped-flow fluorescence for tRNA accommodation, peptide-bond formation assays (puromycin quench or electrophoretic peptide detection), and toeprinting assays to quantify ribosomal positions. (3) Single-molecule FRET: donor-labeled aa-tRNA acceptor-labeled 40S shoulder to monitor shoulder movement and factor dissociation; dwell-time traces collected for ≥500 binding events per condition. Constructs and mutants: WT GTPBP1; ΔN (residues 1–152 deletion); H-loop truncation/replacement with canonical α2 helix; K-pocket coordinate mutations (e.g., coordinating residue -> Ala); catalytic controls (His256Ala); GTPBP2 WT and engineered GTPBP1-like N-domain swap. Baselines: eEF1A wild-type under identical buffer and Mg2+/K+ conditions; GDPCP-locked complexes as non-hydrolyzable baseline; GTPBP2 as paralog baseline. Evaluation metrics: GTP hydrolysis rate k_cat (s^-1), pre- and post-hydrolysis factor dissociation rate k_off (s^-1), tRNA accommodation rate k_acc (s^-1), peptide-bond formation rate k_pep (s^-1), single-molecule dwell times and dwell-time distributions, misincorporation frequency (fraction incorrect peptide products per elongation cycle), cryo-EM class occupancies (%) for pre-delivery, SRL-docked (GTPase-activated), GDP-bound, and accommodated A-site states, and high-resolution map features of mutated sites. Experimental setup: maintain physiological-like ionic conditions (2.5 mM free Mg2+, 100 mM K+), perform cryo-EM sample vitrification per time point with rapid mixing/plunge freezing for GTP datasets, process maps to obtain ensemble of states and quantify state occupancies using classification-of-transferred-heterogeneity (CTH) or equivalent. Biochemical assays run in parallel on identical reconstituted systems; stopped-flow and smFRET performed at 25–37°C with replicate N≥3 independent preparations. Comparison/ablation studies: (A) ΔN vs WT to quantify change in k_off, k_acc, misincorporation; (B) H-loop swap to test restoration of rapid dissociation and reduced fidelity; (C) K-pocket mutation and varying K+ concentrations to test ion-dependence of dissociation kinetics; (D) eEF1A baseline and GTPBP2 comparison to dissociate paralog-specific behaviors. Data analysis: fit kinetic traces to single- or multi-exponential models, compute confidence intervals via bootstrap, and compare groups with paired statistical tests (e.g., t-test or ANOVA with correction). Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Cryo-EM heterogeneity and low population of specific transient states may prevent high-resolution reconstruction of all key intermediates; time-resolved sampling may not capture short-lived activated states. 2) In vitro reconstituted ribosome systems may not replicate cellular cofactor concentrations, post-translational modifications, or crowding that affect GTPBP1 behavior; results may not generalize to in vivo contexts. 3) Mutations (ΔN, H-loop swaps, K-pocket) may cause global misfolding or loss of stability, confounding interpretation of altered kinetics as direct mechanistic effects. 4) Ionic condition dependence (Mg2+, K+) and buffer composition can bias observed kinetics and structural states; physiological ion speciation is difficult to reproduce exactly. 5) Single-molecule and stopped-flow assays require labeling that can perturb native interactions and yield artifacts. 6) Computational classification (CTH) and model fitting may misassign particle states without sufficient particle counts, introducing quantitative uncertainty in state occupancies. 7) Paralog comparisons (GTPBP2) may be limited by differences in expression, folding, or inability to form stable ternary complexes under identical conditions. 8) Scalability: time-resolved cryo-EM and smFRET require substantial instrument time and replicates, limiting throughput for broad mutational scans. 9) The causal link between in vitro fidelity measures and physiological phenotypes (e.g., neurodevelopmental disease) may remain indirect.
